≡ ¬(¬q) ∨ ¬p (Double negation)

≡ ¬(¬p) ∧ ¬q (De Morgan's law)
≡ p ∧ ¬q (Double negation) = RHS. Hence Proved.

title: Show that ¬(p ∨ (¬p ∧ q)) and ¬p ∧ ¬q are logically equivalent by developing a series of logical equivalences.
chunks:
We start with the LHS:
¬(p ∨ (¬p ∧ q))
≡ ¬p ∧ ¬(¬p ∧ q) (De Morgan's law)
≡ ¬p ∧ (¬(¬p) ∨ ¬q) (De Morgan's law)
≡ ¬p ∧ (p ∨ ¬q) (Double negation law)
≡ (¬p ∧ p) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q) (Distributive law)
≡ F ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q) (Negation law)
≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q (Identity law)
This is exactly the RHS. Hence proved.

title: Solve the following recurrence relation: a_n = 11a_{n-1} - 38a_{n-2} + 40a_{n-3}, subject to a_0 = 3, a_1 = 9, a_2 = 27.
chunks:
Characteristic equation: r^3 - 11r^2 + 38r - 40 = 0. Roots: 2, 4, 5.
General solution: an = c12n + c24n + c35n.
Using conditions, solving 3 equations gives the constants for the exact solution.

title: Solve the following recurrence relation by using generating function: a_n = 2a_{n-1} + 3a_{n-2} given a_0 = 1, a_1 = 2
chunks:
Let G(x) be the generating function. G(x) - 1 - 2x = 2x(G(x) - 1) + 3x^2 G(x).
G(x)(1 - 2x - 3x^2) = 1 ⇒ G(x) = 1 / ((1 - 3x)(1 + x)).
Using partial fractions: 1 / ((1 - 3x)(1 + x)) = A / (1 - 3x) + B / (1 + x) gives A = 3/4, B = 1/4.
Solution: an = (3/4)3n + (1/4)(-1)n.

title: Solve the following recurrence relation: a_{n+3} - 5a_{n+2} + 8a_{n+1} - 4a_n = 0 given a_1 = 1, a_2 = 4, a_3 = 11
chunks:

General solution: an = c1 + (c2 + c3n)2n.

title: Solve the following recurrence relation: a_n = 8a_{n-1} - 21a_{n-2} + 18a_{n-3}, subject to a_0 = 1, a_1 = 5, a_2 = 19.

General solution: an = c12n + (c2 + c3n)3n.
Conditions: c1 + c2 = 1, 2c1 + 3(c2 + c3) = 5, 4c1 + 9(c2 + 2c3) = 19. Solving gives constants c1, c2, c3.

title: Solve the following recurrence relation by using generating function: a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2} given a_0 = 0, a_1 = 1
chunks:
This is the Fibonacci sequence.
Let G(x) be the generating function. G(x) - x = x G(x) + x^2 G(x).
G(x)(1 - x - x^2) = x ⇒ G(x) = x / (1 - x - x^2).
Using partial fractions with roots of 1 - x - x^2 = 0, we get Binet's formula: an = (1/√5) [ ((1+√5)/2)n - ((1-√5)/2)n ].

title: Define the following terms with graphs: (i) Complete Bipartite Graph (ii) Complete graph
chunks:
(i) Complete Bipartite Graph: A bipartite graph $G=(V, E)$ with partition $V = V_1 \cup V_2$ is a complete bipartite graph if every vertex in $V_1$ is connected to every vertex in $V_2$. Denoted as $K_{m,n}$ where $m=|V_1|$ and $n=|V_2|$.
(ii) Complete graph: A simple graph in which every pair of distinct vertices is connected by a unique edge. A complete graph on $n$ vertices is denoted as $K_n$.

title: Draw the following graphs: (i) K_5 (ii) C_4

title: State the Handshaking Theorem.
chunks: The Handshaking Theorem states that in any undirected graph, the sum of the degrees of all vertices is equal to twice the number of edges. Mathematically, $\sum_{v \in V} deg(v) = 2|E|$. As a consequence, the number of vertices with an odd degree must be even.

title: Determine the types of following graphs.
chunks:
(i) This graph has parallel edges between a and b, and b and d. Thus, it is a multigraph.
(ii) This directed graph has self-loops (on a, c, e) and directed edges. It is a directed pseudograph.

title: A graph has 6 vertices with degrees 3, 3, 4, 2, 2, 2. Verify whether such a graph can exist, and if it does, find the total number of edges.
chunks:
According to the Handshaking Theorem, the sum of degrees of all vertices equals $2|E|$.
Sum of degrees = 3 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 16.
Since the sum is even, such a graph can exist.
Total number of edges $|E| = 16 / 2 = 8$.

title: (a) A graph has 15 edges. It has one vertex of degree 6, two vertices of degree 5 each, and three vertices of degree 4 each. All remaining vertices have degree 1. Find the total number of vertices in the graph. (b) A graph has 6 vertices with degrees 2,3,4,2,5,x. If the graph has 10 edges, find x.
chunks:
(a) Total edges $|E| = 15$. Sum of degrees = $2 \times 15 = 30$.
Given degrees: one vertex of 6, two of 5, three of 4. Let the number of vertices of degree 1 be $k$.
Sum = $6 + 2(5) + 3(4) + k(1) = 6 + 10 + 12 + k = 28 + k$.
So, $28 + k = 30 \implies k = 2$.
Total vertices = $1 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 8$.
(b) Total edges $|E| = 10$. Sum of degrees = 20.
Sum of given degrees = $2+3+4+2+5+x = 16+x$.
So, $16+x = 20 \implies x = 4$.

Unit I: Propositional Logic CO1

Logic Operators 

NameSymbolMeaning

Conjunctionp ∧ qAND

Tautology & Contradiction 

Tautology: A proposition that is always True (e.g., p ∨ ¬p).

Contradiction: A proposition that is always False (e.g., p ∧ ¬p).

Contingency: A proposition that can be True or False depending on truth values.

Conditionals 

For a conditional statement p → q:

TypeForm

Converseq → p

Inverse¬p → ¬q

Contrapositive¬q → ¬p

Note: p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p (Logically equivalent to contrapositive)

Key Logical Equivalences 

De Morgan's¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q
¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q

Implicationp → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q

Double Negation¬(¬p) ≡ p

Biconditionalp ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)
Unit II: Counting Methods CO2

Permutations & Combinations 

Permutation (Order matters):
 nPr = n! / (n-r)!

Combination (Order doesn't matter):
 nCr = n! / (r!(n-r)!)

Identity: nCr = nCn-r

Linear Homogeneous Recurrences 

Form: an = c1an-1 + c2an-2 + ... + ckan-k

Degree/Order: k (number of previous terms involved)

Characteristic Eq: rk - c1rk-1 - ... - ck = 0

Solving Recurrences (Roots) 

Based on roots of the Characteristic Equation:

RootsGeneral Solution

Distinct (r1 ≠ r2)an = c1r1n + c2r2n

Repeated (r1 = r2)an = (c1 + c2n)r1n

Multiplicity man = (c1 + c2n + ... + cmnm-1)r1n

Generating Functions 

For a sequence a0, a1, a2..., G(x) = Σ anxn

Sequence 1, 1, 1, ...: G(x) = 1 / (1 - x)

Sequence 1, 2, 3, ...: G(x) = 1 / (1 - x)2

Sequence an: G(x) = 1 / (1 - ax)

Fibonacci Sequence: G(x) = x / (1 - x - x2)
Unit III: Graph Theory CO3

Complete & Bipartite Graphs 

Complete Graph (Kn): Every pair of vertices is connected by a unique edge. Edges = n(n-1)/2.

Bipartite Graph: Vertices can be partitioned into V1 and V2 such that every edge connects V1 to V2.

Complete Bipartite (Km,n): Every vertex in V1 connects to every vertex in V2. Edges = m × n.

Handshaking Theorem 

Σ deg(v) = 2|E|

The sum of degrees of all vertices is always even (twice the number of edges).

The number of vertices with an odd degree must be even.

Graph Matrices 

Adjacency Matrix (A): Square matrix. Aij = number of edges between vi and vj.

Incidence Matrix (M): Rows = vertices, Columns = edges. Mij = 1 if edge ej is incident on vi.

Graph Isomorphism 

Two graphs G1 and G2 are isomorphic if they share the same structure. They must have the same:

Number of vertices and edges

Degree sequence (list of vertex degrees)

Number of cycles of same length
